title: The Donation Receipt I Did Not Post
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] After a flood in another district, I donated through a registered relief organization and received a digital receipt.
Narrator: A friend suggested posting the receipt so others would know the campaign was real and might contribute too.
Narrator: [carefully] I understood the possible benefit, but I first asked the organization what information could safely be shared and whether public posting was actually useful.
Narrator: The receipt displayed my full name, reference number, payment details, and the amount. Those details did not belong in a public story.
Narrator: [reflective] The organization said it had already published verified appeal information, audited updates, and safe ways for donors to confirm its work.
Narrator: I shared the official appeal link instead of my receipt, and I removed personal data from any private confirmation I kept for records.
Narrator: [honestly] I also avoided telling people that my contribution had “saved” anyone. A donation is a means, not proof that I know the outcome or another person’s need better than they do.

Narrator: Later, a colleague asked whether I could help him choose a relief group. We checked registration, contact details, published reports, current need, delivery partners, fees, and fraud warnings.
Narrator: [seriously] We did not send money to a new account number forwarded in a chat simply because the message used an emotional photograph.
Narrator: The colleague chose to donate anonymously, while another team member asked the organization whether she could mention the campaign to her community without identifying recipients.
Narrator: [gently] Both choices could be sincere when the purpose, privacy, evidence, and dignity of affected people were protected.
Narrator: I kept the receipt for accounting and tax questions where applicable, but not as a measure of my worth or a claim on anyone’s gratitude.
Narrator: [encouraging] Giving quietly can protect intention, yet discretion must not become secrecy that hides fraud or prevents necessary accountability.
Narrator: The balance is to use trustworthy records and transparent organizations while refusing to turn people’s hardship into a display of our generosity.

quiz.question: Why was the receipt not posted?
options: It contained personal payment and reference information

quiz.question: What did the narrator share instead?
quiz.explanation: Public information came from the organization.

quiz.question: What did the colleague check?
options: Registration, reports, need, fees, delivery, and fraud warnings

quiz.question: Why avoid claiming to save people?
options: A donor cannot know or own every outcome of aid

quiz.question: What balance closes the story?
options: Transparent accountability without displaying hardship or generosity
quiz.explanation: Giving needs both dignity and verification.

quiz.question: Why was the receipt kept private?
What did the narrator share?
options: Verified appeal information from the organization
quiz.explanation: Public information came from the source.

quiz.question: Which fraud signal did they reject?
options: A new account number forwarded only through chat
quiz.explanation: Emotion does not verify payment details.

quiz.question: Why retain a private receipt?
options: It may be needed for accounting without becoming self-display
quiz.explanation: Record keeping has a limited purpose.

quiz.question: When can discretion become harmful?
options: When a donor keeps a receipt
When it conceals fraud or prevents accountability
